sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Glute Ham Raise is a posterior chain exercise performed on a dedicated GHR machine that targets the hamstrings and glutes through knee flexion and hip extension.

Widely used by powerlifters, sprinters, and athletes, this exercise builds exceptional hamstring strength through the full range of motion, from hip extension to knee flexion.

It is one of the most effective exercises for developing the hamstrings and reducing the risk of hamstring injuries.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Targets the hamstrings through both hip extension and knee flexion
- Builds exceptional posterior chain strength
- Reduces the risk of hamstring strains and tears
- Improves sprinting speed and athletic performance
- No external load required — bodyweight provides sufficient resistance
- Strengthens the glutes, lower back, and calves simultaneously
- Excellent for correcting quad-dominant movement patterns

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Hamstrings (Biceps Femoris, Semitendinosus, Semimembranosus), Gluteus Maximus

Secondary: Erector Spinae, Calves (Gastrocnemius), Core (stabilisation)

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Position yourself face down on the glute ham raise machine.
2. Secure your feet firmly under the footpads with the pad resting against your Achilles tendon or lower calves.
3. Position your thighs on the thigh pad so your knees are just below the pad.
4. Cross your arms over your chest or hold them behind your head.
5. Start with your torso hanging perpendicular to the floor.
6. Engage your core before beginning the movement.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Engage your glutes and hamstrings to lift your torso upward.
2. Drive through the footpads, using your hamstrings to curl your body up.
3. Continue raising until your body forms a straight line from head to heels.
4. Squeeze your glutes and hamstrings hard at the top position.
5. Slowly lower your body back down to the starting position under control.
6. Maintain tension in the hamstrings throughout the entire lowering phase.
7. Repeat for the desired number of reps.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Using momentum or swinging to get the body up
- Hyperextending the lower back at the top of the movement
- Not controlling the eccentric (lowering) phase
- Positioning the knees too far forward or backward on the pad
- Letting the hips pike or sag during the movement
- Not engaging the glutes — relying solely on the lower back
- Attempting the full movement before building adequate hamstring strength
- Rushing through reps without maintaining tension

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Glute Ham Raise (GHR) Machine
- Optional: Weight Plate (held at chest for added resistance)
- Optional: Resistance Band (for assistance or added difficulty)
- Recommended: Ensure the machine is properly adjusted before starting

sections.heading: Machine Setup
sections.content:
1. Adjust the footplate so your feet are firmly secured under the pads.
2. The pad should rest against your Achilles tendon or lower calves.
3. Position the thigh pad so your knees sit just below the edge of the pad.
4. This allows the knees to bend freely during the movement.
5. The machine should be stable and secure on the floor.
6. Test the setup with a partial rep before performing a full set.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Feet: Firmly secured under the footpads, toes pointed downward.
2. Knees: Positioned just below the thigh pad for free flexion.
3. Thighs: Resting on the pad for support.
4. Hips: Aligned with the body, not piked or sagging.
5. Arms: Crossed over the chest or behind the head.
6. Core: Braced throughout to maintain a rigid torso.
7. Head: Neutral alignment with the spine.
8. Back: Straight — avoid rounding or hyperextending.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Romanian Deadlift: Hip hinge movement targeting hamstrings and glutes
- Nordic Hamstring Curl: Bodyweight knee flexion for hamstring eccentric strength
- Lying Leg Curl: Machine-based hamstring isolation exercise
- Good Morning: Barbell hip hinge for posterior chain development
- Reverse Hyperextension: Machine exercise targeting glutes and lower back
- Stability Ball Hamstring Curl: Bodyweight alternative using a Swiss ball

sections.heading: Glute Ham Raise Variations
sections.content:
Bodyweight Glute Ham Raise: Standard version with no added resistance
Weighted Glute Ham Raise: Holding a plate at the chest for added load
Banded Glute Ham Raise: Band around the back for accommodating resistance
Assisted Glute Ham Raise: Using a band for support to assist the concentric phase
Slow Tempo Glute Ham Raise: 3-5 second eccentric for maximum time under tension
Glute Ham Raise with Twist: Adding a rotation at the top for oblique engagement

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Cannot Complete Full Rep: Use a resistance band for assistance or perform negatives only
Knee Discomfort: Ensure the pad is positioned correctly below the knee joint
Lower Back Pain: Focus on glute engagement and avoid hyperextending at the top
Hamstring Cramping: Build up volume gradually, stretch before and after
No GHR Machine: Use a Nordic curl setup or stability ball hamstring curls
Beginner: Start with partial reps or band-assisted reps and progress gradually
